newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: New Irish govt could face a rate rise - analysts.
newsitem.headline: New Irish govt could face a rate rise - analysts.

text.p: Ireland's next government will be the envy of many when its takes charge of a booming economy, well on course to meet the entry criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU), after Friday's election.
But the outlook is not all rosy and the new government could face an interest rate rise as well as some tough decisions on the currency when it assumes office, analysts said.
A combination of a weak Irish pound and strong credit growth may prompt the central bank to raise rates to choke inflation once the election is out of the way, they said.

Figures released on Thursday showed no sign of a slowdown in Ireland's lending boom, with annual private sector credit growth at the end of April at 19 percent, toward the top end of market expectations.

The Irish pound has fallen sharply in recent weeks, fuelling fears of imported price inflation. It is down by over five percent on a trade-weighted basis since the start of the year and is hovering near six-year lows against sterling, below 0.9100 pounds.

The central bank said in its recent quarterly bulletin that there were latent pressures pointing to a rise in inflation in the second half of the year. It already raised interest rates by 50 basis points on May 1.
Analysts say that if the currency falls further, particularly if it drops below the key 0.9000 level against sterling, the bank could well move again.

"The bottom line is that if the effective exchange rate index continues to weaken, the bank will move in and push up interest rates again, probably by another 0.5 percent," said Alan McQuaid, economist at Bloxham Stockbrokers.

"Indeed, the only thing stopping the bank from pushing up rates is that it is the eve of the election. Once the election is out of the way, it would be no great surprise if rates were pushed up again, possibly as early as next week."
Other analysts say May inflation data, due for release next week, as well as the performance of the Irish pound, will be crucial in determining the direction of Irish interest rates.

"If we saw a higher than expected CPI figure for May then you would have expectations in the market place that the sterling/Irish rate couldn't go much below 90 pence and you would have an upward movement of market rates," John Beggs, economist at AIB Group Treasury, told Reuters.

The punt has fallen victim in recent weeks to sterling and dollar strength and the belief that it will enter the European single currency below current levels, around its ERM central rate of 2.4100 marks.
Some dealers and analysts say the only way to put a stop to the one-way bet that the EMU entry rate play represents may be to revalue the punt upwards in the ERM.
This has been regarded as an unpalatable option for a government facing an election given its impact on crucial lobby groups, such as farmers and exporters.
But with the election out of the way, the new government may have more room to manoeuvre and may have to look at the issue again if the punt continues to weaken, analysts say.

"A decision on whether to revalue the pound upwards within the European currency system may be one of the first tasks facing the new government," said Austin Hughes, economist at Irish Intercontinental Bank.
